outlooks.summary: Numerous severe storms with damaging winds as the primary hazard are expected during the late afternoon and evening across parts of the Upper Midwest.

sections.title: Upper Midwest
sections.text: An active severe weather period may unfold during the late afternoon and evening, with potential for a derecho and/or significant severe. Further upgrades in probabilities/risk are possible in later outlooks. Large-scale mid-level height falls will spread across the Upper Midwest this afternoon and evening as a significant piece of the northern Rockies trough ejects towards the Red River Valley. This feature is expected to maintain a southwesterly low-level jet into southeast MN and southern WI with ample boundary-layer moisture characterized by lower 70s surface dew points. Robust surface heating is anticipated in the wake of morning elevated convection over eastern IA/WI to a slow-moving cold front that bisects MN to a surface cyclone over southeast SD. The presence of a stout elevated mixed layer will yield a strongly unstable air mass by peak heating with MLCAPE of 2500-3500 J/kg across IA, southern MN and most of WI. Convergence near the surface cyclone in conjunction with increasing mid-level ascent through a minor perturbation approaching from the NE Panhandle and larger-scale height falls should result in deepening convection by 20-21Z across the Siouxland region. sections.title: SD
sections.text: In the wake of the early-day mid-level impulse, strongest surface heating is expected from the NE Panhandle south. Despite more modest surface heating north, yielding only weak buoyancy, ascent associated with the primary shortwave trough should aid in a few surface-based storms in the Black Hills region towards 20-21Z. Highly elongated hodographs will support a couple eastward-moving, potentially long-lived supercells with an attendant severe hail/wind risk. Uncertainty exists in the degree of destabilization east of the Black Hills with guidance varying markedly as this region remains northwest of the surface front. Nevertheless, given the very favorable deep-layer shear profiles, have upgraded to SLGT risk for hail/wind. ..Grams/Peters.. 08/27/2018

sections.title: Upper Midwest Region
sections.text: A broad synoptic trough will continue slowly east through the Rocky Mountain region and northern High Plains today. Preceding this feature, a shortwave trough currently over NE/SD will continue northeast through the upper MS Valley and Great Lakes region this afternoon and evening. As of late morning a slow moving cold front extends from northeast MN southwest through southeast SD into NE. A very moist warm sector resides south of this boundary with low 70s F dewpoints beneath steep mid-level lapse rates indicated on the Aberdeen and Minneapolis 12Z RAOB data. Objective analysis indicates a corridor of 2000 J/kg MLCAPE from southern MN into northern WI, and further destabilization is likely along/south of the front this afternoon. Numerous storms are already in progress in association with the lead shortwave trough from northeast NE into eastern SD primarily in baroclinic zone north of the cold front. Hail is possible with the early storms. With time the forcing for ascent attending the shortwave trough will spread east and overtake the western fringe of the unstable warm sector, and additional storms will likely develop from eastern SD into southwest MN. outlooks.summary: Numerous thunderstorms, some severe with damaging winds and large hail, will move across the upper Great Lakes region this evening. Isolated strong/severe storms are possible farther west into central South Dakota.

sections.title: Discussion
sections.text: Well-defined MCS has evolved over western WI this evening ahead of a pronounced short-wave trough that is expected to eject into the upper Great Lakes tonight. This convection is propagating quickly northeast at speeds in excess of 35-40kt. 00z soundings ahead of this activity exhibit modest instability with adequately sheared flow for the continued maintenance of a well-organized MCS through mid-late evening. In the wake of this activity, severe threat has decreased markedly across MN and for this reason have lowered probabilities except near the IA border. Upstream, convection that developed off the Black Hills is moving east at roughly 40-45kt. Large hail is noted with the strongest storms over Lyman County SD. This convection is expected to spread toward southeastern SD over the next several hours with an attendant threat for hail/wind. ..Darrow.. 08/28/2018

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Storms have increased a bit from the northeast Nebraska vicinity northeast into southwest Minnesota, with risk for marginal hail possible. The need for WW issuance, however, still appears to be a couple of hours off.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: The latest surface analysis depicts a surface front extending from northeast Minnesota southwest across southeast South Dakota, to a weak frontal wave analyzed in northeast Nebraska. Water vapor imagery shows ascent -- associated with a short-wave trough exiting northeast Colorado -- spreading into eastern South Dakota/eastern Nebraska, which has supported some new cell development as well as updraft strengthening within the ongoing band of convection from eastern Nebraska into southwest Minnesota. The storms appear to be limited to the cool side of the boundary at this time, and thus hail likely would be the primary severe risk with a stronger updraft or two, in the short term. Eventually, the moist/destabilizing airmass near and ahead of the surface front in conjunction with increasing ascent will allow surface-based convection to take root, possibly evolving out of the existing northeast Nebraska convection. With the deep-layer wind field expected to increase with time in conjunction with afternoon destabilization, the evolution toward surface-based storms should eventually pose an increasing wind/hail risk, that will likely require WW issuance. At this point, that evolution appears to be a couple of hours in the future, but will continue to monitor short-term trends with respect to ongoing convection, for any possibility that WW issuance may become needed sooner rather than later.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Storms continue to gradually increase, in conjunction with associated severe risk. WW issuance is expected within the next hour or so.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Continued progression of a mid-level short-wave trough across South Dakota/Nebraska is resulting in a steady increase in ascent -- focused near the surface front extending from the western shore of Lake Superior southwest into south central Nebraska. Diurnal heating of the moist pre-frontal boundary layer has resulted in 2500 to 3000 j/Kg mixed-layer CAPE, as indicated by objective analyses, which is supporting a gradual increase in convection -- mainly near and just to the cool side of the boundary. This increase includes a supercell near the immediate frontal zone now crossing southern Mille Lacs county, where risk for mainly hail is evident. Recent MPX special RAOB data shows that the warm-sector boundary layer remains capped, as the suppressed pre-frontal cu field -- per the latest visible satellite loop -- would imply. However, current expectations are for storms to gradually increase near the front -- over the central Minnesota to northern Iowa vicinity -- in the next couple of hours. With the uncontaminated OAX (Omaha, NE) VWP showing moderately strong southwest above-surface flow suggestive of potential for both organized and fast-moving bands of storms, as well as supercells, increasing risks for damaging winds and hail -- along with a possible tornado or two depending upon storm mode/evolution -- suggest that WW will be required in the next 1-2 hours.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: A few isolated supercells will be possible from the Black Hills into central Nebraska. Large hail will be the primary threat. Storm coverage is expected to remain isolated. A WW is not anticipated, but trends in coverage will continue to be monitored.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: As mid-level ascent continues to overspread the area, a few isolated supercell thunderstorms may develop along and near a stationary boundary from the Black Hills southeastward into central Nebraska. 18Z UNR sounding shows very elongated hodograph with steep mid-level lapse rates favorable for large hail. While the 18Z UNR sounding did show some capping left to overcome, modifying the sounding for recent surface observations in the vicinity suggests that some areas may be close to removing MLCIN. The biggest uncertainty will be storm coverage. The current thinking is that coverage will remain isolated to a few areas where the cap can be overcome. Given these concerns, a WW is not currently anticipated. However, should storm coverage increase, a WW will be possible.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Storms are expected to continue east out of Minnesota and progress across Wisconsin and parts of the Upper Peninsula of Michigan. Damaging winds will be the primary threat.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: A shortwave trough and surface low will translate northeast out of southern MN across a moist and unstable air mass, with strengthening mean wind fields through the evening. This should support the expansion and intensification of a line of storms as it develops northeastward. A few embedded areas of rotation are possible within the line, potentially enhancing corridors of wind damage.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Isolated to scattered supercells are expected through the evening. The primary threat will be large hail. A severe thunderstorm watch is possible.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Two supercells have developed east of Rapid City within the last hour. These supercells have produced hail up to golf ball size within the past 30 minutes. Expect the ongoing storms to continue to move eastward along the instability gradient and persist for several more hours. With MUCAPE around 1500 J/kg and deep layer shear around 70 knots per UDX VWP, expect this activity to continue to pose a large hail threat as it moves east. Farther south, additional storm development is possible, but activity should remain more isolated due to weak forcing. However, any storms which can organize will likely be supercells with a threat of large hail and damaging winds given MLCAPE around 2500 to 3500 J/kg and deep layer shear around 45 to 50 knots per LNX VWP. A severe thunderstorm watch may be needed shortly. The best chance for a severe thunderstorm watch will be southern South Dakota ahead of the ongoing supercells which are expected to persist.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: The cluster of storms moving across southern South Dakota may continue to pose a threat of isolated large hail for the next hour or two.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: The earlier supercells have now congealed into a cluster as they moved east across watch 355. This cluster still has the potential for occasional large hail for the next hour or two before it weakens further. Without stronger forcing or low-level jet support, do not expect the severe threat to continue much longer into the overnight period. Therefore, a downstream weather watch is not expected.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: The threat for a few severe wind gusts persists across the watch, and may affect parts of northern Lower Michigan later this evening.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Two lines of storms currently exist across the region. One line was surging northeastward across Upper Michigan, with another trailing southwestward from near Green Bay into southwest Wisconsin. The greatest threat for damaging winds currently appears to be with the more meridionally oriented portion of the line from Green Bay to north of Milwaukee, while storms farther southwest are more oriented along with the deep-layer mean wind. While the strongest instability exists across southern Wisconsin into Iowa, the threat appears to be transitioning to heavy rain with training echoes. To the east, instability is less over northern Michigan, but perhaps sufficient for severe wind gusts given ample shear and mean wind speeds. Depending on convective trends over the next 1-2 hours as storms cross Lake Michigan, a new watch may need to be considered. ..Jewell.. 08/28/2018 ...Please see www.spc.noaa.gov for graphic product...

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Occasional storm intensification capable of producing severe hail may continue into daybreak near/west and southwest through east of Sioux Falls SD. A watch is not anticipated, but trends will continue to be monitored.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: The next in a series of short wave perturbations emerging from the Northwest is now progressing across Wyoming, and associated downstream lower/mid tropospheric warm advection is supporting ongoing increase in thunderstorm activity across the mid Missouri Valley. Activity appears focused roughly along a thermal gradient around the 700 mb level, on the northern periphery of a plume of elevated mixed-layer air emanating from the Great Basin. Storms are elevated above a cold front, with the surface-based stable layer likely to deepen further with the front forecast to continue surging southward across the mid Missouri Valley and central Plains through daybreak and beyond. While the front advances southward, forcing for convective development will continue to develop northeastward along the mid-level front into the 12-14Z time frame. With negligible risk for convection becoming rooted in a moist unstable boundary layer, severe weather potential appears limited. However, given the presence of strong shear and CAPE up to around 1500 J/kg in the convective layer, periodic stronger storm development accompanied by a risk for severe hail may persist several more hours, before the quality of elevated moisture return begins to wane resulting in weakening destabilization.
